blocks.en: 📖 Radical Christianity: The Ten Commandments of Jesus — Unit 6: Be Forgiving
blocks.es_reference: 📖 Cristianismo Radical: Los Diez Mandamientos de Jesús — Unidad 6: Sed Perdonadores

blocks.en: Professor: Dr. Wayne Cook | Director: Dr. Ted Rogers
blocks.es_reference: Profesor: Dr. Wayne Cook | Director: Dr. Ted Rogers

blocks.en: "For if you forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you." — Matthew 6:14 (NKJV)
blocks.es_reference: "Porque si perdonáis a los hombres sus ofensas, os perdonará también a vosotros vuestro Padre celestial." — Mateo 6:14 (RVG)

blocks.en: 1. New Wine in Old Wineskins
blocks.es_reference: 1. Vino Nuevo en Odres Viejos

blocks.en: Matthew 6:14-15 (NKJV): "For if you forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you. But if you do not forgive men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses."
blocks.es_reference: Mateo 6:14-15 (RVG): "Porque si perdonáis a los hombres sus ofensas, os perdonará también a vosotros vuestro Padre celestial; mas si no perdonáis a los hombres sus ofensas, tampoco vuestro Padre os perdonará vuestras ofensas."

blocks.en: Few commands of Jesus are as searching as this one, because He ties our being forgiven to our forgiving. This is not because forgiveness can be earned, but because a heart that has truly received God's mercy cannot hold tightly to its own grudges; refusing to forgive is the sign of a heart that has not yet grasped how much it has been forgiven. To be a Christian is, among other things, to become a forgiving person.
blocks.es_reference: Pocos mandamientos de Jesús escudriñan tanto como éste, porque ata nuestro ser perdonados a nuestro perdonar. No es que el perdón pueda ganarse, sino que un corazón que de veras ha recibido la misericordia de Dios no puede aferrarse a sus propios rencores; negarse a perdonar es la señal de un corazón que aún no ha captado cuánto se le ha perdonado. Ser cristiano es, entre otras cosas, llegar a ser una persona que perdona.

blocks.en: Jesus once said you cannot pour new wine into old wineskins. The old skins of the natural heart are bitterness, the appetite for revenge, and cold indifference toward those who wrong us. The new wine is a forgiveness that flows from grace — and it cannot be contained in the brittle old skins of resentment. This unit follows three movements of that new wine, all drawn straight from Jesus' own teaching: forgiving our enemies, praying for our enemies, and turning the other cheek.
blocks.es_reference: Jesús dijo una vez que no se puede echar vino nuevo en odres viejos. Los odres viejos del corazón natural son la amargura, el apetito de venganza, y la fría indiferencia hacia quienes nos agravian. El vino nuevo es un perdón que fluye de la gracia — y no puede contenerse en los frágiles odres viejos del rencor. Esta unidad sigue tres movimientos de ese vino nuevo, todos tomados directamente de la enseñanza de Jesús: perdonar a nuestros enemigos, orar por nuestros enemigos, y poner la otra mejilla.

blocks.en: 2. What Forgiveness Is — and Is Not
blocks.es_reference: 2. Lo Que el Perdón Es — y No Es

blocks.en: Before we follow those three movements, we should be clear about what forgiveness actually means, because the word is badly misunderstood. To forgive is to release a debt — to give up our claim to repayment and revenge, and to hand the matter over to God, who judges justly. It does not mean pretending the wrong never happened, calling evil good, or feeling a warm rush of affection toward someone who has hurt us. Those misunderstandings make forgiveness sound dishonest or impossible, and so people refuse it.
blocks.es_reference: Antes de seguir esos tres movimientos, conviene tener claro qué significa de veras el perdón, porque la palabra es muy mal entendida. Perdonar es soltar una deuda — renunciar a nuestro derecho al pago y a la venganza, y entregar el asunto a Dios, que juzga con justicia. No significa fingir que el agravio nunca ocurrió, llamar bueno al mal, ni sentir una cálida oleada de afecto hacia quien nos ha herido. Esos malentendidos hacen que el perdón suene deshonesto o imposible, y por eso la gente lo rechaza.

blocks.en: Real forgiveness is more honest than that. It looks the wrong full in the face, names it as wrong, and then chooses not to repay it. It is something we do before we feel it, an act of the will rooted in grace rather than a feeling we must wait for. And it is finally a matter of obedience and freedom: the bitterness we nurse against another person harms us far more than it harms them, and forgiveness is how we are set free from that poison.
blocks.es_reference: El perdón verdadero es más honesto que eso. Mira el agravio de frente, lo nombra como agravio, y luego decide no devolverlo. Es algo que hacemos antes de sentirlo, un acto de la voluntad arraigado en la gracia más que un sentimiento que debamos esperar. Y es al final cuestión de obediencia y de libertad: la amargura que guardamos contra otra persona nos daña mucho más a nosotros que a ella, y el perdón es como somos librados de ese veneno.

blocks.en: 3. The New Wine of Forgiving Our Enemies
blocks.es_reference: 3. El Vino Nuevo de Perdonar a Nuestros Enemigos

blocks.en: Matthew 5:43-44 (NKJV): "You have heard that it was said, 'You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy.' But I say to you, love your enemies, bless those who curse you, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who spitefully use you and persecute you."
blocks.es_reference: Mateo 5:43-44 (RVG): "Oísteis que fue dicho: Amarás a tu prójimo, y aborrecerás a tu enemigo. Mas yo os digo: Amad a vuestros enemigos, bendecid a los que os maldicen, haced bien a los que os aborrecen, y orad por los que os ultrajan y os persiguen."

blocks.en: The first movement is the hardest: we are to forgive even our enemies. The old wine said love your neighbor and hate your enemy, and that still feels like simple justice to the natural heart. But Jesus pours new wine: love your enemies, bless those who curse you, do good to those who hate you. This is not weakness; it is the supernatural mark of a child of God, who makes His sun rise on the evil and the good alike.
blocks.es_reference: El primer movimiento es el más difícil: hemos de perdonar aun a nuestros enemigos. El vino viejo decía ama a tu prójimo y aborrece a tu enemigo, y eso todavía le parece simple justicia al corazón natural. Pero Jesús echa vino nuevo: amad a vuestros enemigos, bendecid a los que os maldicen, haced bien a los que os aborrecen. Esto no es debilidad; es la marca sobrenatural de un hijo de Dios, que hace salir su sol sobre malos y buenos por igual.

blocks.en: The Cree chief: Maskepetoon, a Cree chief who had come to Christ, learned that a man of the Blackfoot tribe had murdered his father. He rode for the man, and everyone expected revenge. Instead he said, "You have killed my father, so now you must be my father. You shall ride my best horse and wear my best clothes." The stunned man fell to his knees: "My son, now you have killed me!" Forgiveness had done what revenge never could — it ended the hatred.
blocks.es_reference: El jefe cree: Maskepetoon, un jefe cree que había venido a Cristo, supo que un hombre de la tribu de los pies negros había asesinado a su padre. Cabalgó en busca del hombre, y todos esperaban venganza. En cambio dijo: "Has matado a mi padre, así que ahora debes ser mi padre. Montarás mi mejor caballo y vestirás mi mejor ropa." El hombre, atónito, cayó de rodillas: "¡Hijo mío, ahora me has matado!" El perdón había hecho lo que la venganza nunca pudo — puso fin al odio.

blocks.en: That is the power of the new wine. Revenge only multiplies the wound; forgiveness alone can actually end the cycle. We see the same lesson in General Robert E. Lee after the Civil War, who told a bitter widow that it was better to forget the injustices of the past than to let them poison the rest of her life — "cut it down and forget it." Bitterness clung to becomes a poison we drink ourselves.
blocks.es_reference: Ése es el poder del vino nuevo. La venganza solo multiplica la herida; solo el perdón puede de veras romper el ciclo. Vemos la misma lección en el general Robert E. Lee tras la Guerra Civil, quien dijo a una viuda amargada que era mejor olvidar las injusticias del pasado que dejarlas envenenar el resto de su vida — "córtalo y olvídalo." La amargura retenida se vuelve un veneno que bebemos nosotros mismos.

blocks.en: 4. The Witness of Those Who Forgave
blocks.es_reference: 4. El Testimonio de los Que Perdonaron

blocks.en: This new wine is not a modern sentiment; it runs all through Scripture, in people who forgave when they had every earthly right to retaliate. Joseph, sold into slavery by his own brothers, told them, "you meant evil against me; but God meant it for good," and provided for them instead of avenging himself (Genesis 50). Stephen, while being stoned to death, prayed, "Lord, do not charge them with this sin" (Acts 7). David, with King Saul hunting his life, twice held the power to kill him and twice spared him (1 Samuel 24). Paul and Silas, beaten and jailed, stayed to lead their jailer to Christ rather than escape (Acts 16).
blocks.es_reference: Este vino nuevo no es un sentimiento moderno; corre por toda la Escritura, en personas que perdonaron cuando tenían todo derecho humano de tomar represalia. José, vendido como esclavo por sus propios hermanos, les dijo: "vosotros pensasteis mal contra mí, mas Dios lo encaminó a bien," y proveyó para ellos en vez de vengarse (Génesis 50). Esteban, mientras lo apedreaban hasta morir, oró: "Señor, no les imputes este pecado" (Hechos 7). David, perseguido a muerte por el rey Saúl, dos veces tuvo el poder de matarlo y dos veces lo perdonó (1 Samuel 24). Pablo y Silas, azotados y encarcelados, se quedaron para llevar a su carcelero a Cristo en vez de huir (Hechos 16).

blocks.en: Above all of them stands the Lord Himself, who prayed from the cross, "Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they do" (Luke 23:34). This is the deepest reason we forgive: we are only passing on what we ourselves have received. The Christian forgives an enemy not because the enemy deserves it, but because Christ forgave us when we did not deserve it. Forgiveness is grace flowing downhill.
blocks.es_reference: Por encima de todos está el Señor mismo, que oró desde la cruz: "Padre, perdónalos, porque no saben lo que hacen" (Lucas 23:34). Ésta es la razón más honda por la que perdonamos: solo transmitimos lo que nosotros mismos hemos recibido. El cristiano perdona a un enemigo no porque el enemigo lo merezca, sino porque Cristo nos perdonó cuando no lo merecíamos. El perdón es gracia que corre cuesta abajo.

blocks.en: 5. The New Wine of Praying for Our Enemies
blocks.es_reference: 5. El Vino Nuevo de Orar por Nuestros Enemigos

blocks.en: Luke 6:28 (NKJV): "bless those who curse you, and pray for those who spitefully use you."
blocks.es_reference: Lucas 6:28 (RVG): "bendecid a los que os maldicen, y orad por los que os calumnian."

blocks.en: The second movement turns forgiveness into something active. Jesus does not merely tell us to stop cursing those who wrong us; He tells us to pray for them. The old wine is gossip, muttered curses, and silent resentment that rehearses the offense again and again. The new wine is intercession — actually carrying the person who hurt us before God and asking for their good.
blocks.es_reference: El segundo movimiento convierte el perdón en algo activo. Jesús no solo nos dice que dejemos de maldecir a quienes nos agravian; nos dice que oremos por ellos. El vino viejo es el chisme, las maldiciones murmuradas, y el rencor callado que ensaya la ofensa una y otra vez. El vino nuevo es la intercesión — llevar de veras ante Dios a la persona que nos hirió y pedir por su bien.

blocks.en: There is deep wisdom in this command, for it is nearly impossible to keep hating someone you are sincerely praying for. Prayer slowly changes the one who prays. As we lift an enemy to God, our own heart begins to soften, and the person we resented becomes, in our eyes, another struggling soul whom God loves. Praying for an enemy is how forgiveness takes root and grows rather than remaining a one-time decision we soon forget.
blocks.es_reference: Hay profunda sabiduría en este mandamiento, pues es casi imposible seguir odiando a alguien por quien oras sinceramente. La oración poco a poco cambia al que ora. Al levantar a un enemigo ante Dios, nuestro propio corazón empieza a ablandarse, y la persona que resentíamos se vuelve, a nuestros ojos, otra alma que lucha y a quien Dios ama. Orar por un enemigo es como el perdón echa raíz y crece en vez de quedar como una decisión única que pronto olvidamos.

blocks.en: 6. The New Wine of Turning the Other Cheek
blocks.es_reference: 6. El Vino Nuevo de Poner la Otra Mejilla

blocks.en: Matthew 5:38-39 (NKJV): "You have heard that it was said, 'An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth.' But I tell you not to resist an evil person. But whoever slaps you on your right cheek, turn the other to him also."
blocks.es_reference: Mateo 5:38-39 (RVG): "Oísteis que fue dicho: Ojo por ojo, y diente por diente. Mas yo os digo: No resistáis al malo; antes a cualquiera que te hiera en tu mejilla derecha, vuélvele también la otra."

blocks.en: The third movement is the most misread. To grasp it we have to picture the scene Jesus described. A blow to the right cheek, delivered by a right-handed person, is a backhand — and in that culture a backhand was not how you fought an equal but how a superior insulted an inferior, a master striking a servant. To turn the other cheek is not cowering passivity; it is to stand and offer the left cheek, which can only be struck with an open hand, the way one strikes an equal. It quietly forces the aggressor to confront the humanity of the person he is abusing. Turning the other cheek is dignified, nonviolent resistance — refusing both to retaliate and to be degraded.
blocks.es_reference: El tercer movimiento es el más malentendido. Para captarlo hay que imaginar la escena que Jesús describió. Un golpe en la mejilla derecha, dado por un diestro, es un revés — y en aquella cultura un revés no era cómo se peleaba con un igual sino cómo un superior insultaba a un inferior, un amo golpeando a un siervo. Poner la otra mejilla no es una pasividad temerosa; es ponerse de pie y ofrecer la mejilla izquierda, que solo puede golpearse con la mano abierta, como se golpea a un igual. Obliga calladamente al agresor a enfrentar la humanidad de la persona que maltrata. Poner la otra mejilla es resistencia digna y no violenta — negarse a la vez a tomar represalia y a ser degradado.

blocks.en: Kuldeep Singh: An Indian customs officer named Kuldeep Singh slapped Pastor John across the face on several occasions over a period of days. The pastor never retaliated. When the officer later fell gravely ill with tuberculosis and was dying, Pastor John came to him, wept over him, and prayed for him. The man recovered, and in the face of such returned good he became a Christian. Grace, not retaliation, broke through where force never could.
blocks.es_reference: Kuldeep Singh: Un oficial de aduanas de la India llamado Kuldeep Singh abofeteó al pastor John en el rostro en varias ocasiones a lo largo de unos días. El pastor nunca tomó represalia. Cuando el oficial más tarde cayó gravemente enfermo de tuberculosis y agonizaba, el pastor John vino a él, lloró por él, y oró por él. El hombre se recuperó, y ante semejante bien devuelto se hizo cristiano. La gracia, no la represalia, abrió paso donde la fuerza nunca pudo.

blocks.en: 7. Not a Doormat: The Guardrail
blocks.es_reference: 7. No un Felpudo: La Salvaguarda

blocks.en: Here we must guard against a serious misunderstanding, because this teaching has often been twisted to keep victims silent. Turning the other cheek does not mean becoming a doormat for endless abuse. Jesus Himself, when struck unjustly at His trial, did not silently offer another blow; He challenged the man: "If I have spoken evil, bear witness of the evil; but if well, why do you strike Me?" (John 18:23). Setting a boundary, removing oneself from danger, or seeking justice through proper means is not the same as taking revenge.
blocks.es_reference: Aquí debemos guardarnos de un grave malentendido, porque esta enseñanza a menudo se ha torcido para callar a las víctimas. Poner la otra mejilla no significa volverse un felpudo para el abuso sin fin. El mismo Jesús, cuando lo golpearon injustamente en su juicio, no ofreció en silencio otro golpe; desafió al hombre: "Si he hablado mal, da testimonio del mal; y si bien, ¿por qué me golpeas?" (Juan 18:23). Poner un límite, apartarse del peligro, o buscar justicia por los medios debidos no es lo mismo que tomar venganza.

blocks.en: The boxer-evangelist: A converted Irish boxer was heckled and then struck twice by a troublemaker while he was raising a gospel tent. He calmly counted the two blows, then rolled up his sleeves and said, "The Lord gave me no further instructions." It is told with a smile, but the point is real: non-retaliation is not a license for others to abuse us without limit.
blocks.es_reference: El boxeador evangelista: A un boxeador irlandés convertido lo hostigaron y luego lo golpearon dos veces mientras levantaba una carpa para predicar. Contó con calma los dos golpes, luego se arremangó y dijo: "El Señor no me dio más instrucciones." Se cuenta con una sonrisa, pero el punto es real: la no represalia no es una licencia para que otros nos abusen sin límite.

blocks.en: So forgiveness and boundaries are not enemies. We forgive fully, releasing the debt and the desire for revenge, while still acting wisely to stop ongoing harm. Ending unjust treatment is not vengeance; refusing to nurse bitterness is not the same as pretending nothing happened. The new wine frees us both from the urge to retaliate and from the lie that love requires us to be destroyed.
blocks.es_reference: Así que el perdón y los límites no son enemigos. Perdonamos plenamente, soltando la deuda y el deseo de venganza, mientras seguimos actuando con sabiduría para detener el daño en curso. Poner fin a un trato injusto no es venganza; negarse a alimentar la amargura no es lo mismo que fingir que nada pasó. El vino nuevo nos libra a la vez del impulso de tomar represalia y de la mentira de que el amor exige que nos destruyan.

blocks.en: 8. Practical Tools for a Forgiving Heart
blocks.es_reference: 8. Herramientas Prácticas para un Corazón Que Perdona

blocks.en: Scripture also gives down-to-earth help for living this out in the heat of the moment. First, the gentle answer: "a soft answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger" (Proverbs 15:1) — as Abigail's gentle words turned David from violence (1 Samuel 25). Second, delay your reaction: "let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath" (James 1:19); when Jesus was asked to condemn the woman caught in sin, He paused and stooped to write before answering (John 8). The pause is often where grace gets its foothold.
blocks.es_reference: La Escritura también da ayuda concreta para vivir esto en el calor del momento. Primera, la respuesta amable: "la blanda respuesta quita la ira; mas la palabra áspera hace subir el furor" (Proverbios 15:1) — como las palabras amables de Abigail apartaron a David de la violencia (1 Samuel 25). Segunda, demora tu reacción: "todo hombre sea pronto para oír, tardo para hablar, tardo para airarse" (Santiago 1:19); cuando le pidieron a Jesús que condenara a la mujer sorprendida en pecado, se detuvo y se inclinó a escribir antes de responder (Juan 8). La pausa es a menudo donde la gracia encuentra su punto de apoyo.

blocks.en: Third, learn to overlook the small things: "the discretion of a man makes him slow to anger, and it is to his glory to overlook a transgression" (Proverbs 19:11). Not every slight needs a response; much of peace is simply letting little offenses go. There is an old story of President Lincoln counseling an angry colleague to write out his furious letter in full — and then to put it in the stove and never send it. The writing relieved the anger; the stove prevented the damage.
blocks.es_reference: Tercera, aprende a pasar por alto las cosas pequeñas: "la cordura del hombre detiene su furor; y su honra es disimular la ofensa" (Proverbios 19:11). No toda ofensa necesita respuesta; gran parte de la paz es sencillamente dejar pasar las pequeñas ofensas. Hay una vieja historia del presidente Lincoln, que aconsejó a un colega airado que escribiera por completo su carta furiosa — y luego la metiera en la estufa y nunca la enviara. Escribirla alivió la ira; la estufa evitó el daño.

blocks.en: 9. A New Creation
blocks.es_reference: 9. Una Nueva Criatura

blocks.en: All of this comes back to the wineskins. "If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation; old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new" (2 Corinthians 5:17). You cannot pour the new wine of forgiveness into the old wineskins of resentment and revenge; the old skins must go. Becoming a forgiving person is not a matter of trying harder to be nice. It is the overflow of a heart remade by grace, that has tasted God's mercy and can no longer hoard its grudges.
blocks.es_reference: Todo esto vuelve a los odres. "Si alguno está en Cristo, nueva criatura es; las cosas viejas pasaron; he aquí todas son hechas nuevas" (2 Corintios 5:17). No se puede echar el vino nuevo del perdón en los odres viejos del rencor y la venganza; los odres viejos deben irse. Llegar a ser una persona que perdona no es cuestión de esforzarse más por ser amable. Es el desbordamiento de un corazón rehecho por la gracia, que ha probado la misericordia de Dios y ya no puede atesorar sus rencores.

blocks.en: So the command stands, and it turns out to be a gift: forgive, and you will be forgiven; pray for those who wrong you, and watch your own bitterness dissolve; refuse both revenge and degradation, and walk free. The same Lord who prayed "Father, forgive them" pours His own new wine into every heart that will receive it, and makes us, at last, people who forgive.
blocks.es_reference: Así que el mandamiento permanece, y resulta ser un regalo: perdona, y serás perdonado; ora por los que te agravian, y mira tu propia amargura disolverse; rehúsa a la vez la venganza y la degradación, y anda libre. El mismo Señor que oró "Padre, perdónalos" echa su propio vino nuevo en todo corazón que quiera recibirlo, y nos hace, al fin, personas que perdonan.

mc.stem: In Matthew 6:14-15, how does Jesus connect our forgiving to God's forgiving?
options: Forgiveness can be earned by works
If we forgive others, our Father will forgive us; if we do not, neither will He
mc.why: Jesus ties the two together: a heart that has truly received mercy cannot hoard grudges; refusing to forgive shows a heart that has not grasped its own forgiveness.

mc.stem: What is the 'old wine' of the natural heart, according to the lesson?
options: Bitterness, the appetite for revenge, and cold indifference
mc.why: The old wineskins of the natural heart are bitterness, the appetite for revenge, and cold indifference; the new wine is forgiveness flowing from grace.

mc.stem: According to the lesson, what does forgiveness actually mean?
options: Releasing a debt — giving up our claim to repayment and revenge
Feeling warm affection for the offender
mc.why: To forgive is to release a debt, giving up our claim to repayment and revenge and handing the matter to God — not pretending or feeling affection.

mc.stem: The lesson says forgiveness is primarily what?
options: A feeling we must wait for
An act of the will rooted in grace, done before we feel it
Something only the offender can start
mc.why: Forgiveness is something we do before we feel it — an act of the will rooted in grace, not a feeling we must wait for.

mc.stem: What is the 'new wine' Jesus pours regarding our enemies (Matthew 5:43-44)?
options: Love your neighbor and hate your enemy
Love your enemies, bless those who curse you, do good to those who hate you
mc.why: The old wine said love neighbor and hate enemy; Jesus pours new wine: love your enemies, bless those who curse you, do good to those who hate you.

mc.stem: How did the converted Cree chief Maskepetoon respond to his father's murderer?
options: He said, 'You must now be my father; ride my best horse and wear my best clothes'
mc.why: Instead of revenge, the chief made the murderer his 'father,' giving his best horse and clothes; the stunned man knelt, and forgiveness ended the hatred.

mc.stem: What did General Robert E. Lee counsel the bitter widow after the Civil War?
options: To forget the injustices of the past rather than let them poison the rest of her life
mc.why: Lee said it was better to forget past injustices than to let them poison the rest of one's life — 'cut it down and forget it.'

mc.stem: According to the lesson, what is the deepest reason a Christian forgives an enemy?
options: Because Christ forgave us when we did not deserve it — grace flowing downhill
mc.why: We forgive not because the enemy deserves it but because Christ forgave us undeserving — we pass on the grace we received.

mc.stem: Which biblical figure prayed, 'Lord, do not charge them with this sin,' while being killed?
mc.why: Stephen, while being stoned, prayed that the sin not be charged against his killers (Acts 7) — a witness of the new wine of forgiveness.

mc.stem: What is the 'new wine' of the second movement (Luke 6:28)?
options: Praying for and interceding for those who wrong us
mc.why: The second movement turns forgiveness active: not just ceasing to curse, but actually praying for and interceding for those who wrong us.

mc.stem: Why does praying for an enemy change us, according to the lesson?
options: It is nearly impossible to keep hating someone you sincerely pray for
It guarantees they will be punished
It forces the enemy to apologize
mc.why: Prayer slowly changes the one who prays; it is nearly impossible to keep hating someone you sincerely pray for, and the heart softens.

mc.stem: In Jesus' day, what did a backhand slap to the right cheek signify?
options: An insult from a superior to an inferior, like a master striking a servant
mc.why: A backhand to the right cheek was not how one fought an equal but how a superior insulted an inferior — a master striking a servant.

mc.stem: According to the lesson, what does turning the other cheek actually do?
options: Forces the aggressor to confront the equal humanity of the one he abuses — dignified nonviolent resistance
mc.why: Offering the left cheek can only be struck as an equal; it is dignified, nonviolent resistance that confronts the aggressor with the victim's humanity.

mc.stem: How did Pastor John respond to Kuldeep Singh, who had repeatedly slapped him?
options: When the officer was dying, John wept over him and prayed; the man recovered and became a Christian
mc.why: When Kuldeep Singh lay dying of TB, Pastor John came and prayed for him; he recovered and became a Christian — grace broke through where force could not.

mc.stem: What crucial guardrail does the lesson place on 'turning the other cheek'?
options: It does not mean being a doormat; setting boundaries and seeking justice is not revenge
mc.why: Turning the cheek is not becoming a doormat; setting boundaries, removing oneself from danger, or seeking lawful justice is not the same as revenge.

mc.stem: How does the lesson show even Jesus did not silently accept an unjust blow?
options: At His trial He challenged the man: 'If I have spoken evil, bear witness; but if well, why do you strike Me?'
mc.why: Struck unjustly at His trial, Jesus challenged the man rather than offering another blow (John 18:23) — showing the guardrail against being a doormat.

mc.stem: What practical tool does Proverbs 15:1 give for a forgiving heart?
options: A soft answer turns away wrath
mc.why: A soft answer turns away wrath (Prov 15:1) — as Abigail's gentle words turned David from violence; gentleness defuses anger.

mc.stem: What does the Abraham Lincoln 'unsent letter' story teach?
options: Write out the anger if needed, but then put it in the stove — relieve it without doing damage
mc.why: Lincoln counseled writing the furious letter and then burning it: the writing relieved the anger, while the stove prevented the damage.

mc.stem: What does Proverbs 19:11 commend as 'to a man's glory'?
options: To overlook a transgression — letting small offenses go
mc.why: It is to a man's glory to overlook a transgression (Prov 19:11); not every slight needs a response, and much of peace is letting little offenses go.

mc.stem: How does 2 Corinthians 5:17 ground the whole call to be forgiving?
options: By demanding harder effort to be nice
Forgiveness is the overflow of a new creation — new wine can't go in old wineskins of resentment
By removing the command to forgive
mc.why: In Christ we are a new creation; forgiveness is the overflow of a heart remade by grace, not mere effort — new wine cannot go in old wineskins of resentment.

sa.prompt: Explain how Matthew 6:14-15 connects our forgiving others to God's forgiving us.
sa.model: In Matthew 6 Jesus says that if we forgive others their trespasses our heavenly Father will forgive us, but if we do not forgive, neither will He forgive us. This is searching because it ties our being forgiven to our forgiving. It does not mean forgiveness can be earned, but that a heart which has truly received God's mercy cannot hold tightly to its own grudges. Refusing to forgive is the sign of a heart that has not yet grasped how much it has been forgiven. To be a Christian is, among other things, to become a forgiving person, because the mercy we have received naturally flows out toward others.

sa.prompt: Using the wineskins image, contrast the old wine and the new wine of this unit.
sa.model: Jesus said you cannot pour new wine into old wineskins, and the lesson uses that to frame forgiveness. The old wineskins of the natural heart are bitterness, the appetite for revenge, and a cold indifference toward those who wrong us. The new wine is a forgiveness that flows from grace, and it cannot be contained in the brittle old skins of resentment. The unit follows three movements of that new wine, all from Jesus' own teaching: forgiving our enemies, praying for our enemies, and turning the other cheek. Becoming forgiving is not trying harder to be nice but letting the old skins go so the new wine of grace can fill us.

sa.prompt: What does forgiveness actually mean, and what does it NOT mean?
sa.model: To forgive is to release a debt, giving up our claim to repayment and revenge and handing the matter over to God who judges justly. It does not mean pretending the wrong never happened, calling evil good, or feeling a warm rush of affection toward the one who hurt us; those misunderstandings make forgiveness sound dishonest or impossible. Real forgiveness is more honest than that, for it looks the wrong full in the face, names it as wrong, and then chooses not to repay it. It is an act of the will rooted in grace, done before we feel it, and it is finally a matter of obedience and freedom, since the bitterness we nurse harms us more than the offender and forgiveness sets us free from that poison.

sa.prompt: Describe the first movement (forgiving enemies) and how the Cree chief illustrates it.
sa.model: The first and hardest movement is to forgive even our enemies. The old wine said love your neighbor and hate your enemy, but Jesus pours new wine: love your enemies, bless those who curse you, do good to those who hate you. This is not weakness but the supernatural mark of a child of God, who makes His sun rise on evil and good alike. The converted Cree chief Maskepetoon illustrates it: when a Blackfoot man murdered his father, he rode for revenge, but instead said the man must now be his father, and gave him his best horse and clothes. The stunned man knelt, crying that the chief had now killed him, for forgiveness had done what revenge never could and ended the hatred.

sa.prompt: Name several biblical figures who forgave, and explain the deepest reason Christians forgive.
sa.model: The new wine runs all through Scripture in people who forgave when they had every right to retaliate. Joseph told the brothers who sold him that they meant evil but God meant it for good, and provided for them. Stephen, while being stoned, prayed that the sin not be charged against his killers. David twice spared King Saul when he could have killed him. Paul and Silas stayed to save their jailer rather than escape. Above them all, Jesus prayed from the cross, Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they do. This is the deepest reason we forgive: we are only passing on what we have received, forgiving an enemy not because the enemy deserves it but because Christ forgave us when we did not deserve it, so that forgiveness is grace flowing downhill.

sa.prompt: Explain the second movement, praying for our enemies, and why it changes us.
sa.model: The second movement turns forgiveness into something active, for Jesus does not merely tell us to stop cursing those who wrong us but to pray for them. The old wine is gossip, muttered curses, and silent resentment that rehearses the offense again and again. The new wine is intercession, actually carrying the person who hurt us before God and asking for their good. There is deep wisdom in this, because it is nearly impossible to keep hating someone you are sincerely praying for. Prayer slowly changes the one who prays, so that as we lift an enemy to God our own heart softens and the person we resented becomes, in our eyes, another struggling soul whom God loves. Praying for an enemy is how forgiveness takes root and grows rather than fading as a one-time decision.

sa.prompt: Explain the cultural meaning of the Roman backhand slap and what turning the other cheek really does.
sa.model: To grasp the third movement we must picture the scene. A blow to the right cheek by a right-handed person is a backhand, and in that culture a backhand was not how you fought an equal but how a superior insulted an inferior, a master striking a servant. To turn the other cheek is not cowering passivity; it is to stand and offer the left cheek, which can only be struck with an open hand, the way one strikes an equal. This quietly forces the aggressor to confront the humanity of the person he is abusing. Turning the other cheek is therefore dignified, nonviolent resistance, refusing both to retaliate and to be degraded. It neither returns the blow nor accepts the insult, but insists on the dignity God gives.

sa.prompt: Why is turning the other cheek NOT being a doormat? Use the guardrail and Jesus' own example.
sa.model: We must guard against a serious misunderstanding, because this teaching has often been twisted to keep victims silent. Turning the other cheek does not mean becoming a doormat for endless abuse. Jesus Himself, when struck unjustly at His trial, did not silently offer another blow but challenged the man, asking why he struck Him if He had spoken well. Setting a boundary, removing oneself from danger, or seeking justice through proper means is not the same as taking revenge. So forgiveness and boundaries are not enemies: we forgive fully, releasing the debt and the desire for revenge, while still acting wisely to stop ongoing harm. Ending unjust treatment is not vengeance, and refusing to nurse bitterness is not pretending nothing happened. The new wine frees us from the urge to retaliate and from the lie that love requires us to be destroyed.

sa.prompt: Describe the three practical tools Scripture gives for a forgiving heart.
sa.model: Scripture gives down-to-earth help for the heat of the moment. First, the gentle answer: a soft answer turns away wrath but a harsh word stirs up anger, as Abigail's gentle words turned David from violence. Second, delay your reaction: let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath, and remember that when Jesus was asked to condemn the woman caught in sin He paused and stooped to write before answering, for the pause is often where grace gets its foothold. Third, learn to overlook the small things, since it is to a man's glory to overlook a transgression and not every slight needs a response. There is an old story of Lincoln counseling an angry colleague to write out his furious letter and then put it in the stove and never send it, so the writing relieved the anger while the stove prevented the damage.

sa.prompt: How does 2 Corinthians 5:17 (new creation) ground the whole call to be forgiving?
sa.model: All of this comes back to the wineskins, for Paul says that if anyone is in Christ he is a new creation, the old things have passed away and all things have become new. You cannot pour the new wine of forgiveness into the old wineskins of resentment and revenge; the old skins must go. Becoming a forgiving person is therefore not a matter of trying harder to be nice but the overflow of a heart remade by grace, that has tasted God's mercy and can no longer hoard its grudges. So the command turns out to be a gift: forgive and you will be forgiven, pray for those who wrong you and watch your bitterness dissolve, refuse both revenge and degradation and walk free. The same Lord who prayed Father forgive them pours His new wine into every heart that will receive it and makes us at last people who forgive.
